r0.why: Medium-grained, from shale-like rock [1]; pronounced schistosity [2]; grains visible with hand lens, splits into flakes or plates [3]; Greek schizein 'to split' [12].

r1.why: Platy minerals listed [4], interleaved granular quartz/feldspar [5], 0.25-2 mm grains [16], over half oriented [17], porphyroblasts such as garnet very often [23].

r2.why: Elevated temperature and unequal compression [30], typical of regional metamorphism with mountain building [31], perpendicular to greatest compression as platy minerals rotate or recrystallise [32].

r3.why: Clay to mica [36], mudstone to slate to phyllite [37], then medium-grained mica schist [38], dehydration to granular minerals, less schistosity, gneiss [39].

r4.why: Defined by texture, makeup varies greatly [19]; mudstones and tuffs [7]; chlorite and talc schist from ultramafic igneous rocks [41]; graphite schist uncommon, from organic-carbon-rich beds [43].

r5.why: Protolith naming with schistose metasandstone [9], otherwise mineral names [10], quartz-feldspar-biotite schist of uncertain protolith [28], civil engineering challenge from planes of weakness [11].
